claim: Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) establishes a latent infection in neurons and periodically reactivates to cause disease.
source: Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) establishes a latent infection in neurons and periodically reactivates to cause disease.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by extensive prior research and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: HSV-1 reactivation from latently infected mouse neurons induced by forskolin requires neuronal excitation.
source: We demonstrate HSV-1 reactivation from latently infected mouse neurons induced by forskolin requires neuronal excitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing that inhibition of neuronal excitation blocks forskolin-mediated reactivation.

claim: Stimuli that directly induce neurons to become hyperexcitable also induced HSV-1 reactivation.
source: Stimuli that directly induce neurons to become hyperexcitable also induced HSV-1 reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that KCl treatment and TTX-release, which induce hyperexcitability, trigger HSV-1 reactivation.

claim: Forskolin-induced reactivation was dependent on the neuronal pathway of DLK/JNK activation.
source: Forskolin-induced reactivation was dependent on the neuronal pathway of DLK/JNK activation and included an initial wave of viral gene expression that was independent of histone demethylase activity and linked to histone phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that DLK and JNK inhibitors block forskolin-mediated reactivation.

claim: Forskolin-induced reactivation included an initial wave of viral gene expression that was independent of histone demethylase activity.
source: Forskolin-induced reactivation was dependent on the neuronal pathway of DLK/JNK activation and included an initial wave of viral gene expression that was independent of histone demethylase activity and linked to histone phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that histone demethylase inhibitors do not block Phase I viral gene expression.

claim: Forskolin-induced reactivation included an initial wave of viral gene expression linked to histone phosphorylation.
source: Forskolin-induced reactivation was dependent on the neuronal pathway of DLK/JNK activation and included an initial wave of viral gene expression that was independent of histone demethylase activity and linked to histone phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing co-localization of viral genomes with H3K9me3/S10p.

claim: IL-1β is released under conditions of stress, fever and UV exposure of the epidermis.
source: IL-1β is released under conditions of stress, fever and UV exposure of the epidermis; all known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on IL-1β release.

claim: Stress, fever and UV exposure of the epidermis are all known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation.
source: IL-1β is released under conditions of stress, fever and UV exposure of the epidermis; all known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of HSV reactivation.

claim: IL-1β induced histone phosphorylation in sympathetic neurons.
source: We found that IL-1β induced histone phosphorylation and increased the excitation in sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased H3K9me3/S10p staining following IL-1β treatment.

claim: IL-1β increased the excitation in sympathetic neurons.
source: We found that IL-1β induced histone phosphorylation and increased the excitation in sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased cytosolic Ca2+ elevations in response to acetylcholine following IL-1β treatment.

claim: IL-1β triggered HSV-1 reactivation.
source: Importantly, IL-1β triggered HSV-1 reactivation, which was dependent on DLK and neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased GFP-positive neurons following IL-1β treatment.

claim: IL-1β-triggered HSV-1 reactivation was dependent on DLK.
source: Importantly, IL-1β triggered HSV-1 reactivation, which was dependent on DLK and neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that DLK inhibition and knockdown block IL-1β-mediated reactivation.

claim: IL-1β-triggered HSV-1 reactivation was dependent on neuronal excitability.
source: Importantly, IL-1β triggered HSV-1 reactivation, which was dependent on DLK and neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that TTX blocks IL-1β-mediated reactivation.

claim: HSV-1 co-opts an innate immune pathway resulting from IL-1 stimulation of neurons to induce reactivation.
source: Thus, HSV-1 co-opts an innate immune pathway resulting from IL-1 stimulation of neurons to induce reactivation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing IL-1β triggers reactivation via neuronal excitability and DLK activation.

claim: HSV-1 is present in approximately 40–90% of the population worldwide.
source: Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) is a ubiquitous human pathogen that is present in approximately 40–90% of the population worldwide (Arvin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: HSV-1 persists for life in the form of a latent infection in neurons, with intermittent episodes of reactivation.
source: HSV-1 persists for life in the form of a latent infection in neurons, with intermittent episodes of reactivation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of HSV biology.

claim: Reactivation from a latent infection and subsequent replication of the virus can cause substantial disease including oral and genital ulcers, herpes keratitis, and encephalitis.
source: Reactivation from a latent infection and subsequent replication of the virus can cause substantial disease including oral and genital ulcers, herpes keratitis, and encephalitis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSV-1 disease manifestations.

claim: Multiple studies have linked persistent HSV-1 infection to the progression of Alzheimer's disease.
source: In addition, multiple studies have linked persistent HSV-1 infection to the progression of Alzheimer's disease (Itzhaki, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Stimuli in humans that are linked to clinical HSV-1 reactivation include exposure to UV light, psychological stress, fever, and changes in hormone levels.
source: Stimuli in humans that are linked to clinical HSV-1 reactivation include exposure to UV light, psychological stress, fever, and changes in hormone levels (Suzich and Cliffe, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: During a latent infection of neurons, there is evidence that the viral genome is assembled into a nucleosomal structure by associating with cellular histone proteins.
source: During a latent infection of neurons, there is evidence that the viral genome is assembled into a nucleosomal structure by associating with cellular histone proteins (Deshmane and Fraser, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The viral lytic promoters have modifications that are characteristic of silent heterochromatin (histone H3 di- and tri-methyl lysine 9; H3K9me2/3, and H3K27me3).
source: The viral lytic promoters have modifications that are characteristic of silent heterochromatin (histone H3 di- and tri-methyl lysine 9; H3K9me2/3, and H3K27me3) (Wang et al., 2005; Knipe and Cliffe, 2008; Cliffe et al., 2009; Kwiatkowski et al., 2009), which is thought to maintain long-term silencing of the viral lytic genes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Heterochromatin modifications on viral lytic promoters are thought to maintain long-term silencing of the viral lytic genes.
source: The viral lytic promoters have modifications that are characteristic of silent heterochromatin (histone H3 di- and tri-methyl lysine 9; H3K9me2/3, and H3K27me3) (Wang et al., 2005; Knipe and Cliffe, 2008; Cliffe et al., 2009; Kwiatkowski et al., 2009), which is thought to maintain long-term silencing of the viral lytic genes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on prior literature and established knowledge.

claim: For reactivation to occur, viral lytic gene expression is induced from promoters that are assembled into heterochromatin and in the absence of viral proteins, such as VP16.
source: Hence, for reactivation to occur, viral lytic gene expression is induced from promoters that are assembled into heterochromatin and in the absence of viral proteins, such as VP16, which are important for lytic gene expression upon de novo infection and full reactivation (Thompson et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VP16 is important for lytic gene expression upon de novo infection and full reactivation.
source: Hence, for reactivation to occur, viral lytic gene expression is induced from promoters that are assembled into heterochromatin and in the absence of viral proteins, such as VP16, which are important for lytic gene expression upon de novo infection and full reactivation (Thompson et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The initiation of viral lytic gene expression, including VP16, during reactivation is dependent on host proteins and the activation of cellular signaling pathways.
source: The initiation of viral lytic gene expression, including VP16, during reactivation is therefore dependent on host proteins and the activation of cellular signaling pathways (Suzich and Cliffe, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: One of the best characterized stimuli of HSV reactivation in primary neuronal models is nerve growth factor (NGF) deprivation and subsequent loss of PI3K/AKT activity.
source: One of the best characterized stimuli of HSV reactivation in primary neuronal models is nerve growth factor (NGF) deprivation and subsequent loss of PI3K/AKT activity (Wilcox and Johnson, 1988; Wilcox et al., 1990; Camarena et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) cell stress response via activation of dual leucine zipper kinase (DLK) was required for reactivation in response to loss of NGF signaling.
source: Previously, we found that activation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) cell stress response via activation of dual leucine zipper kinase (DLK) was required for reactivation in response to loss of NGF signaling (Cliffe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Recent work has identified a role for JNK in HSV reactivation following perturbation of the DNA damage/repair pathways.
source: In addition, recent work has identified a role for JNK in HSV reactivation following perturbation of the DNA damage/repair pathways, which also triggers reactivation via inhibition of AKT activity (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Perturbation of the DNA damage/repair pathways triggers reactivation via inhibition of AKT activity.
source: In addition, recent work has identified a role for JNK in HSV reactivation following perturbation of the DNA damage/repair pathways, which also triggers reactivation via inhibition of AKT activity (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DLK is a master regulator of the neuronal stress response.
source: DLK is a master regulator of the neuronal stress response, and its activation can result in cell death, axon pruning, axon regeneration or axon degeneration depending on the nature of activating trigger (Tedeschi and Bradke, 2013; Geden and Deshmukh, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DLK activation can result in cell death, axon pruning, axon regeneration or axon degeneration depending on the nature of activating trigger.
source: DLK is a master regulator of the neuronal stress response, and its activation can result in cell death, axon pruning, axon regeneration or axon degeneration depending on the nature of activating trigger (Tedeschi and Bradke, 2013; Geden and Deshmukh, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HSV has co-opted the neuronal stress pathway of JNK activation by DLK to induce reactivation.
source: Therefore, it appears that HSV has co-opted this neuronal stress pathway of JNK activation by DLK to induce reactivation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data and prior literature.

claim: One mechanism by which JNK functions to promote lytic gene expression is via a histone phosphorylation on S10 of histone H3.
source: One mechanism by which JNK functions to promote lytic gene expression is via a histone phosphorylation on S10 of histone H3 (Cliffe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: JNK-dependent histone phosphorylation occurs on histone H3 that maintains K9 methylation and is therefore known as a histone methyl/phospho switch.
source: JNK-dependent histone phosphorylation occurs on histone H3 that maintains K9 methylation and is therefore known as a histone methyl/phospho switch, which likely permits viral lytic gene transcription without the requirement for recruitment of histone demethylases (Fischle et al., 2005; Gehani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The histone methyl/phospho switch likely permits viral lytic gene transcription without the requirement for recruitment of histone demethylases.
source: JNK-dependent histone phosphorylation occurs on histone H3 that maintains K9 methylation and is therefore known as a histone methyl/phospho switch, which likely permits viral lytic gene transcription without the requirement for recruitment of histone demethylases (Fischle et al., 2005; Gehani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on citations to prior literature and the experimental data.

claim: The initial wave of viral lytic gene expression is known as Phase I.
source: This initial wave of viral lytic gene expression is known as Phase I, and also occurs independently of the lytic transactivator VP16.
evidence: This is established terminology in the field based on prior work.

claim: Phase I viral lytic gene expression occurs independently of the lytic transactivator VP16.
source: This initial wave of viral lytic gene expression is known as Phase I, and also occurs independently of the lytic transactivator VP16.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature and experimental data.

claim: Late gene expression in Phase I occurs independent of viral genome replication.
source: In addition, late gene expression in Phase I occurs independent of viral genome replication (Kim et al., 2012; Cliffe and Wilson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A sub-population of neurons progress to full reactivation (also known as Phase II), which occurs 48–72 hr post-stimulus.
source: A sub-population of neurons then progress to full reactivation (also known as Phase II), which occurs 48–72 hr post-stimulus and requires both VP16 and histone demethylase activity (Cliffe et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Messer et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2014), and includes viral DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Phase II reactivation requires both VP16 and histone demethylase activity.
source: A sub-population of neurons then progress to full reactivation (also known as Phase II), which occurs 48–72 hr post-stimulus and requires both VP16 and histone demethylase activity (Cliffe et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Messer et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2014), and includes viral DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Phase II reactivation includes viral DNA replication.
source: A sub-population of neurons then progress to full reactivation (also known as Phase II), which occurs 48–72 hr post-stimulus and requires both VP16 and histone demethylase activity (Cliffe et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Messer et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2014), and includes viral DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and experimental data.

claim: The bi-phasic progression has not been observed in some models of reactivation such as axotomy.
source: However, this bi-phasic progression has not been observed in some models of reactivation such as axotomy, which results in more rapid viral gene expression and a dependence on histone demethylase activity for viral gene expression at the earliest time points investigated (Liang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Axotomy results in more rapid viral gene expression and a dependence on histone demethylase activity for viral gene expression at the earliest time points investigated.
source: However, this bi-phasic progression has not been observed in some models of reactivation such as axotomy, which results in more rapid viral gene expression and a dependence on histone demethylase activity for viral gene expression at the earliest time points investigated (Liang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Forskolin has previously been found to induce HSV reactivation.
source: Although forskolin has previously been found to induce HSV reactivation, (Smith et al., 1992; Colgin et al., 2001; De Regge et al., 2010; Danaher et al., 2003), the mechanism by which forskolin induces reactivation is not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism by which forskolin induces reactivation is not known.
source: Although forskolin has previously been found to induce HSV reactivation, (Smith et al., 1992; Colgin et al., 2001; De Regge et al., 2010; Danaher et al., 2003), the mechanism by which forskolin induces reactivation is not known.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Hyperstimulation of cortical neurons following forskolin treatment or potassium chloride mediated depolarization has previously been found to result in a global histone methyl/phospho switch.
source: We turned our attention to forskolin treatment and neuronal hyperexcitability because hyperstimulation of cortical neurons following forskolin treatment or potassium chloride mediated depolarization has previously been found to result in a global histone methyl/phospho switch (Noh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with changes in cellular gene expression.
source: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with changes in cellular gene expression, increased DNA damage (Alt and Schwer, 2018; Madabhushi et al., 2015), and epigenetic changes including H3 phosphorylation (Noh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with increased DNA damage.
source: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with changes in cellular gene expression, increased DNA damage (Alt and Schwer, 2018; Madabhushi et al., 2015), and epigenetic changes including H3 phosphorylation (Noh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with epigenetic changes including H3 phosphorylation.
source: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with changes in cellular gene expression, increased DNA damage (Alt and Schwer, 2018; Madabhushi et al., 2015), and epigenetic changes including H3 phosphorylation (Noh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Forskolin-induced reactivation was dependent on ion-channel activity.
source: Using a variety of small-molecule inhibitors, we found that forskolin-induced reactivation was dependent on ion-channel activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ion channel inhibitors block forskolin-mediated reactivation.

claim: Stimuli that are well established as causing heightened neuronal activity also induced HSV to undergo reactivation.
source: In support of a role for neuronal hyperexcitability causing HSV reactivation, stimuli that are well established as causing heightened neuronal activity also induced HSV to undergo reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that KCl and TTX-release induce reactivation.

claim: DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following hyperstimulation.
source: In addition, DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression, which occurred prior to viral DNA replication and independently of histone demethylase activity, indicating that hyperstimulation-induced reactivation also involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that DLK and JNK inhibitors block Phase I gene expression.

claim: The initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following hyperstimulation occurred prior to viral DNA replication.
source: In addition, DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression, which occurred prior to viral DNA replication and independently of histone demethylase activity, indicating that hyperstimulation-induced reactivation also involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing viral gene expression at 20 hr but DNA replication not until 48 hr.

claim: The initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following hyperstimulation occurred independently of histone demethylase activity.
source: In addition, DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression, which occurred prior to viral DNA replication and independently of histone demethylase activity, indicating that hyperstimulation-induced reactivation also involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that histone demethylase inhibitors do not block Phase I gene expression.

claim: Hyperstimulation-induced reactivation involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
source: In addition, DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression, which occurred prior to viral DNA replication and independently of histone demethylase activity, indicating that hyperstimulation-induced reactivation also involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing two phases of gene expression.

claim: IL-1β is released under conditions of psychological stress and fever.
source: IL-1β is released under conditions of psychological stress and fever (Ericsson et al., 1994; Goshen and Yirmiya, 2009; Koo and Duman, 2009; Saper and Breder, 1994); both known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation (Glaser and Kiecolt-Glaser, 1997; Cohen et al., 1999; Chida and Mao, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Psychological stress and fever are both known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation.
source: IL-1β is released under conditions of psychological stress and fever (Ericsson et al., 1994; Goshen and Yirmiya, 2009; Koo and Duman, 2009; Saper and Breder, 1994); both known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation (Glaser and Kiecolt-Glaser, 1997; Cohen et al., 1999; Chida and Mao, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-1β has previously been found to induce heightened neuronal activity.
source: IL-1β has previously been found to induce heightened neuronal activity (Vezzani and Viviani, 2015; Schneider et al., 1998; Binshtok et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-1β is involved in the extrinsic immune response to infection via activation of neutrophils and lymphocytes.
source: For example, IL-1β is involved in the extrinsic immune response to infection via activation of neutrophils and lymphocytes (Sims and Smith, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: IL-1β can act on non-immune cells including fibroblasts to initiate an antiviral response.
source: In addition, it can act on non-immune cells including fibroblasts to initiate an antiviral response (Orzalli et al., 2018; Aarreberg et al., 2019), as has previously been described for lytic infection with HSV-1 (Orzalli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-1β was capable of inducing reactivation of HSV from mature sympathetic neurons.
source: Interestingly, we found that IL-1β was capable of inducing reactivation of HSV from mature sympathetic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased GFP-positive neurons following IL-1β treatment.

claim: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels impeded reactivation mediated by both forskolin and IL-1β.
source: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels impeded reactivation mediated by both forskolin and IL-1β.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that TTX and ZD 7288 block reactivation.

claim: Activity of the cell stress protein DLK was essential for IL-1β-mediated reactivation.
source: Activity of the cell stress protein DLK was also essential for IL-1β-mediated reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that DLK inhibition and knockdown block IL-1β-mediated reactivation.

claim: IL-1β is a novel trigger for HSV reactivation that acts via neuronal hyperexcitability.
source: We therefore identify IL-1β as a novel trigger from HSV reactivation that acts via neuronal hyperexcitability and highlight the central role of JNK activation by DLK in HSV reactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: JNK activation by DLK plays a central role in HSV reactivation.
source: We therefore identify IL-1β as a novel trigger from HSV reactivation that acts via neuronal hyperexcitability and highlight the central role of JNK activation by DLK in HSV reactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Forskolin treatment induced robust HSV reactivation.
source: We found addition of forskolin but not dd-forskolin triggered robust HSV reactivation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dideoxy-forskolin (dd-forskolin) did not trigger robust HSV reactivation.
source: We found addition of forskolin but not dd-forskolin triggered robust HSV reactivation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment of latently-infected primary neurons with a cAMP mimetic (8-bromo-cAMP) was sufficient to trigger reactivation.
source: Treatment of latently-infected primary neurons with a cAMP mimetic (8-bromo-cAMP) was sufficient to trigger reactivation (Figure 1D), suggesting that increased intracellular levels of cAMP are capable of inducing HSV reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Increased intracellular levels of cAMP are capable of inducing HSV reactivation.
source: Treatment of latently-infected primary neurons with a cAMP mimetic (8-bromo-cAMP) was sufficient to trigger reactivation (Figure 1D), suggesting that increased intracellular levels of cAMP are capable of inducing HSV reactivation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing that a cAMP mimetic triggers reactivation.

claim: Inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity using SQ22,536 significantly diminished HSV reactivation.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity using SQ22, 536 (Haslam et al., 1978) significantly diminished HSV reactivation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Activation of adenylate cyclase, which results in increased intracellular levels of cAMP, is required for robust forskolin-mediated reactivation.
source: Therefore, activation of adenylate cyclase, which results in increased intracellular levels of cAMP, is required for robust forskolin-mediated reactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that adenylate cyclase inhibition blocks reactivation.

claim: Both the JNK and DLK inhibitors prevented forskolin-mediated reactivation based on the number of GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-stimulus.
source: Both the JNK and DLK inhibitors prevented forskolin-mediated reactivation based on the number of GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Forskolin-mediated reactivation is dependent on the neuronal stress pathway mediated by DLK activation of JNK.
source: These data therefore indicate forskolin-mediated reactivation is dependent on the neuronal stress pathway mediated by DLK activation of JNK.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that DLK and JNK inhibitors block reactivation.

claim: Us11-GFP synthesis in neurons started to appear around 48 hr post-forskolin treatment, with more robust reactivation observed at 72 hr.
source: In response to forskolin treatment, Us11-GFP synthesis in neurons started to appear around 48 hr post-reactivation, with more robust reactivation observed at 72 hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Superinfection with a replication competent wild-type virus resulted in a rapid induction of GFP-positive neurons by 24 hr post-superinfection.
source: In contrast to forskolin-mediated reactivation, the number of GFP-positive neurons following superinfection with a replication competent wild-type virus resulted in a rapid induction of GFP-positive neurons by 24 hr post-superinfection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Forskolin-triggered reactivation results in slower synthesis of Us11-GFP than superinfection.
source: Therefore, forskolin-triggered reactivation results in slower synthesis of Us11-GFP than superinfection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the kinetics of GFP expression between forskolin treatment and superinfection.

claim: Forskolin triggers reactivation from only a subpopulation of latently-infected neurons (approximately 1 in every 3.4 neurons compared to superinfection).
source: In addition, these data highlight the ability of forskolin to trigger reactivation from only a subpopulation of latently-infected neurons (approximately 1 in every 3.4 neurons compared to superinfection).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the number of GFP-positive neurons between forskolin treatment and superinfection.

claim: An increase in viral genome copy number was not detected until 48 hr post-forskolin stimulus, which continued between 48 hr and 72 hr.
source: An increase in viral genome copy number was also not detected until 48 hr post-stimulus, which continued between 48 hr and 72 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A significant up-regulation of ICP27, ICP4, ICP8, UL30, UL48, and gC mRNA occurred at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment.
source: For all six transcripts, a significant up-regulation of mRNA occurred at 20 hr post-treatment, including the true late gene gC, whose expression would usually only be stimulated following viral genome replication in the context of de novo lytic replication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Forskolin triggers a Phase I wave of lytic gene expression.
source: Therefore, this indicates that lytic gene expression is induced prior to viral DNA replication and that forskolin does trigger a Phase I wave of lytic gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing viral gene expression before DNA replication.

claim: There was a significant reduction in ICP27, UL30 and gC mRNA levels at 20 hr post-stimulus in the presence of the JNK inhibitor SP600125.
source: We found a significant reduction in ICP27 (2.2-fold), UL30 (3.3-fold) and gC (5.5-fold) mRNA levels at 20 hr post-stimulus in the presence of SP600125 (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Treatment with the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511 resulted in a decrease in ICP27, UL30, and gC mRNAs compared to forskolin treatment alone.
source: We observed comparable results following treatment with the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511, with a 2.3-, 3-, 8.8-fold decrease in ICP27, UL30, and gC mRNAs, respectively, compared to forskolin treatment alone, and no significant increase in mRNA levels compared to the unreactivated samples (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Transduction with DLK targeting shRNA vectors resulted in >90-fold reduction in DLK protein levels compared to the shRNA control transduced neurons.
source: Transduction with the DLK targeting shRNA vectors resulted in >90-fold reduction in DLK protein levels compared to the shRNA control transduced neurons (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: There was a significant reduction in HSV reactivation and ICP27, UL30, and gC mRNA levels at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment following transduction with either DLK shRNA lentivirus compared to the shRNA control transduced neurons.
source: We observed a significant reduction in HSV reactivation and ICP27, UL30, and gC mRNA levels at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment following transduction with either DLK shRNA lentivirus compared to the shRNA control transduced neurons (Figure 2K–L and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K-L and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Addition of a PKA inhibitor (KT 5720) did not inhibit Phase I reactivation.
source: However, using well a characterized inhibitor of PKA (KT 5720), we were unable to find a role for PKA in Phase I reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), although full reactivation was inhibited (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Addition of a PKA inhibitor (KT 5720) inhibited full reactivation.
source: However, using well a characterized inhibitor of PKA (KT 5720), we were unable to find a role for PKA in Phase I reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), although full reactivation was inhibited (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Addition of a CREB inhibitor (666-15) inhibited full reactivation but did not inhibit Phase I gene expression.
source: Although addition of a CREB inhibitor (666-15), inhibited full reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) it did not inhibit Phase I gene expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claim: Inhibition of EPAC1 with ESI09 did not inhibit forskolin-mediated reactivation.
source: However, inhibition of EPAC1 with ESI09 did not inhibit forskolin-mediated reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Addition of SQ22,536 did not prevent reactivation triggered by the cAMP mimetic 8-Bromo-cAMP.
source: Given that we had already found that SQ22,536 inhibited forskolin-mediated reactivation (Figure 1E), to directly test the inhibition of EPAC2 by SQ22,536 in a way that bypasses adenylate cyclase we investigated the effect reactivation induced by 8-Bromo-cAMP. Addition of SQ22,536 did not prevent reactivation triggered by the cAMP mimetic (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Forskolin induces a Phase I wave of gene expression that does not depend on activation of PKA, EPAC1 or EPAC2 but does require DLK and JNK activity.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that forskolin induces a Phase I wave of gene expression that does not depend on activation of PKA, EPAC1 or EPAC2 but does require DLK and JNK activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data with various inhibitors.

claim: Forskolin treatment was associated with an increase in the levels of γH2AX at 5 hr post-treatment, which resolved by 15 hr post-treatment.
source: Forskolin treatment was associated with an increase in the levels of γH2AX at 5 hr post-treatment, which resolved by 15 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C), and is therefore indicative of physiological DNA damage and repair, which occurs upon neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: The increase in γH2AX following forskolin treatment is indicative of physiological DNA damage and repair, which occurs upon neuronal hyperexcitability.
source: Forskolin treatment was associated with an increase in the levels of γH2AX at 5 hr post-treatment, which resolved by 15 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C), and is therefore indicative of physiological DNA damage and repair, which occurs upon neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data and prior knowledge about γH2AX as a marker of DNA damage.

claim: The intensity of nuclear cFOS accumulation increased at 5 hr post-forskolin treatment.
source: To also indirectly probe for neuronal hyperexcitability following forskolin treatment, we also quantified nuclear cFOS accumulation and found that the intensity increased at 5 hr post-forskolin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Forskolin treatment did not result in loss of pAKT measured at 15 hr post-treatment.
source: Although we did observe increased levels of γH2AX following forskolin treatment, we did not detect a concurrent loss of pAKT measured at 15 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), whereas PI3-kinase inhibition by LY294002 did result in loss of pAKT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PI3-kinase inhibition by LY294002 resulted in loss of pAKT.
source: Although we did observe increased levels of γH2AX following forskolin treatment, we did not detect a concurrent loss of pAKT measured at 15 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), whereas PI3-kinase inhibition by LY294002 did result in loss of pAKT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both PI3-kinase inhibition and forskolin treatment resulted in activation of the JNK cell stress pathway, indicated by increased c-Jun phosphorylation.
source: Both PI3-kinase inhibition and forskolin treatment did result in activation of the JNK cell stress pathway, indicated by increased c-Jun phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HSV reactivation and JNK activation in response to forskolin treatment does not involve dephosphorylation of AKT.
source: This indicates that HSV reactivation and JNK activation in response to forskolin treatment does not involve dephosphorylation of AKT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing no loss of pAKT following forskolin treatment.

claim: Hyperexcitability triggers reactivation via an alternative mechanism that does not feed into AKT phosphorylation.
source: Therefore, hyperexcitability triggers reactivation via an alternative mechanism that does not feed into AKT phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing no loss of pAKT following forskolin treatment.

claim: Forskolin triggered a transient increase in H3K9me3/S10p at 5 hr post-treatment that had returned to baseline by 10 hr.
source: Forskolin triggered a transient increase in H3K9me3/S10p at 5 hr post-treatment that had returned to baseline by 10 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Forskolin induces a histone H3K9me3/pS10 methyl/phospho switch on regions on cellular chromatin in sympathetic neurons.
source: This indicates that, in keeping with cortical neurons, forskolin induces a histone H3K9me3/pS10 methyl/phospho switch on regions on cellular chromatin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing increased H3K9me3/S10p following forskolin treatment.

claim: Viral genomes co-localized with H3K9me3/pS10 following forskolin treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 3A and B, viral genomes co-localized with H3K9me3/pS10 following robust H3K9me3/S10p staining at 5 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The percentage of viral genomes that co-localized with H3K9me3/S10p was significantly increased compared to the mock reactivated samples at 5 hr and 20 hr post-forskolin treatment.
source: The percentage of viral genomes that co-localized with H3K9me3/S10p was significantly increased compared to the mock reactivated samples at 5 hr and 20 hr post-forskolin treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LSD1 activity is required for forskolin-mediated reactivation.
source: The addition of two independent LSD1 inhibitors (OG-L002 and S 2102) inhibited Us11-GFP synthesis at 72 hr post-reactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F). Hence, LSD1 activity, and presumably removal of H3K9-methylation, is required for forskolin-mediated reactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: LSD1 inhibition did not prevent the initial induction of ICP27 and gC mRNA expression at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment.
source: However, LSD1 inhibition did not prevent the initial induction of ICP27 and gC mRNA expression at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following forskolin-mediated reactivation is independent of histone H3K9 demethylase activity.
source: Therefore, this initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following forskolin-mediated reactivation is independent of histone H3K9 demethylase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that LSD1 inhibitors do not block Phase I gene expression.

claim: Treatment of neurons with the UTX/JMJD3 inhibitor GSK-J4 prevented the synthesis of Us11-GFP at 72-hr post-reactivation.
source: Treatment of neurons with the UTX/JMJD3 inhibitor GSK-J4 (Kruidenier et al., 2012) prevented the synthesis of Us11-GFP at 72-hr post-reactivation, indicating that removal of K27 methylation is required full reactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Removal of K27 methylation is required for full reactivation.
source: Treatment of neurons with the UTX/JMJD3 inhibitor GSK-J4 (Kruidenier et al., 2012) prevented the synthesis of Us11-GFP at 72-hr post-reactivation, indicating that removal of K27 methylation is required full reactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that GSK-J4 blocks full reactivation.

claim: The initial burst of gene expression (assessed by ICP27 and gC mRNA levels) was robustly induced at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment in the presence of GSK-J4.
source: However, the initial burst of gene expression (assessed by ICP27 and gC mRNA levels) was robustly induced at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment in the presence of GSK-J4 (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The initial phase of gene expression following forskolin treatment is independent of histone demethylase activity and consistent with a role for a histone methyl/phospho switch in permitting lytic gene expression.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that the initial phase of gene expression following forskolin treatment is independent of histone demethylase activity and therefore consistent with a role for a histone methyl/phospho switch in permitting lytic gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that histone demethylase inhibitors do not block Phase I gene expression.

claim: The addition of TTX significantly inhibited HSV reactivation triggered by forskolin.
source: The addition of TTX significantly inhibited HSV reactivation triggered by forskolin, as measured by Us11-GFP-positive neurons at 72-hr post-stimulus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The addition of tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocked HSV reactivation measured by Us11-GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-forskolin treatment.
source: The addition of tetraethylammonium (TEA), which inhibits voltage-gated potassium channel activity, also blocked HSV reactivation measured by Us11-GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-forskolin treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Action potential firing is required for forskolin-mediated reactivation.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that action potential firing is required for forskolin-mediated reactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that inhibitors of action potential firing block reactivation.

claim: Addition of ZD 7288, Ivabradine or CsCl all significantly reduced HSV reactivation triggered by forskolin.
source: Addition of ZD 7288 (Figure 4C), Ivabradine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or CsCl (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) all significantly reduced HSV reactivation triggered by forskolin, as measured by Us-11 GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Expression of ICP27, UL30 and gC mRNAs were significantly decreased in the presence of ZD 7288 compared to the forskolin treated neurons alone.
source: Expression of representative lytic mRNAs ICP27 (Figure 4D), UL30 and gC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D) were significantly decreased in the presence of ZD 7288 compared to the forskolin treated neurons alone, and were not significantly increased compared to the mock treated samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Addition of ZD 7288 resulted in significantly decreased staining intensities of both H3K9me3/S10p and γH2AX at 5 hr post-forskolin treatment.
source: Addition of ZD 7288 resulted in significantly decreased staining intensities of both H3K9me3/S10p and γH2AX at 5 hr post-forskolin treatment (Figure 4E and F), which was the peak time-point for which we observed these changes upon forskolin treatment alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and S3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Activity of the HCN channels and/or voltage-gated sodium channels in response to increased levels of cAMP results in hyperexcitability-associated changes in histone modifications and the initial induction of lytic gene expression during Phase I and reactivation of HSV from latent infection.
source: Therefore, activity of the HCN channels and/or voltage-gated sodium channels in response to increased levels of cAMP, results in hyperexcitability-associated changes in histone modifications and the initial induction of lytic gene expression during Phase I and reactivation of HSV from latent infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that HCN and sodium channel inhibitors block reactivation and histone modifications.

claim: Both forskolin and KCl treatments triggered HSV reactivation more robustly if applied for 8 hr or more.
source: Both of these treatments triggered HSV reactivation more robustly if applied for 8 hr or more (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Chronic neuronal hyperexcitability is important in inducing reactivation of HSV.
source: This indicates that chronic neuronal hyperexcitability is important in inducing reactivation of HSV.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that longer treatment times result in more robust reactivation.

claim: Removal from a TTX block resulted in a robust HSV reactivation as determined by Us11-GFP synthesis.
source: TTX was added to the neurons for 2 days and then washed out. This resulted in a robust HSV reactivation as determined by Us11-GFP synthesis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of the JNK inhibitor SP600125 or the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511 blocked HSV reactivation following TTX-release.
source: Addition of the JNK inhibitor SP600125 or the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511 blocked HSV reactivation following TTX-release (Figure 5B) as did shRNA mediated depletion of DLK (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: shRNA mediated depletion of DLK blocked HSV reactivation following TTX-release.
source: Addition of the JNK inhibitor SP600125 or the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511 blocked HSV reactivation following TTX-release (Figure 5B) as did shRNA mediated depletion of DLK (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Directly inducing neuronal hyperexcitability triggers HSV reactivation in a DLK/JNK-dependent manner.
source: Therefore, directly inducing neuronal hyperexcitability triggers HSV reactivation in a DLK/JNK-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that TTX-release induces reactivation that is blocked by DLK/JNK inhibitors.

claim: Exposure of mature neurons to IL-1β induced an accumulation of the hyperexcitability-associated histone post-translational modifications γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p.
source: In sympathetic neurons, we found that exposure of mature neurons to IL-1β induced an accumulation of the hyperexcitability-associated histone post-translational modifications γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: IL-1β did not induce the same changes in γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p for post-natal neurons as it did for mature neurons.
source: We did not observe the same changes for post-natal neurons.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Addition of either TTX or anti-IL1R antibody resulted in a significant reduction in γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p levels in response to IL-1β treatment.
source: Addition of either TTX or anti-IL1R antibody resulted in a significant reduction in γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p levels in response to IL-1β treatment (Figure 6B–C), indicating that the response is directly due to IL1 and requires activity of voltage-gated sodium channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: The response to IL-1β is directly due to IL1 and requires activity of voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: Addition of either TTX or anti-IL1R antibody resulted in a significant reduction in γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p levels in response to IL-1β treatment (Figure 6B–C), indicating that the response is directly due to IL1 and requires activity of voltage-gated sodium channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that TTX and anti-IL1R antibody block the response.

claim: Neurons pre-treated with IL-1β for 20 hr displayed higher elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ as measured by Fura-2-AM compared to mock treated controls.
source: Compared to mock treated controls, neurons that were pre-treated with IL-1β for 20 hr displayed higher elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ as measured by Fura-2-AM, a ratiometric indicator of cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Neurons pre-treated with IL-1β exhibit significantly higher levels of cytosolic Ca2+ in response to acetylcholine compared to untreated controls.
source: Importantly, compared to untreated controls, neurons pre-treated with IL-1β exhibit significantly higher levels of cytosolic Ca2+ in response to acetylcholine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: The increase in acetylcholine responses observed in IL-1β treated neurons was prevented with the addition of the IL1R blocking antibody.
source: The increase in acetylcholine responses observed in IL-1β treated neurons was prevented with the addition of the IL1R blocking antibody, indicating that it is specific for signaling through the IL1 receptor (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The increase in acetylcholine responses in IL-1β treated neurons is specific for signaling through the IL1 receptor.
source: The increase in acetylcholine responses observed in IL-1β treated neurons was prevented with the addition of the IL1R blocking antibody, indicating that it is specific for signaling through the IL1 receptor (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that the IL1R blocking antibody prevents the response.

claim: Addition of IL-1β triggered HSV reactivation in mature neurons quantified by the number of Us11-GFP neurons at 3 days.
source: Addition of IL-1β triggered HSV reactivation in mature neurons quantified by the number of Us11-GFP neurons at 3 days (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Addition of the IL-1R blocking antibody prevented IL-1β induced reactivation.
source: Addition of the IL-1R blocking antibody preventing IL-1β induced reactivation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels by TTX resulted in a significant decrease in the ability of IL-1β to induce reactivation.
source: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels by TTX resulted in a significant decrease in the ability of IL-1β to induce reactivation (Figure 7E), therefore indicating that IL-1β triggered reactivation is via increasing neuronal activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: IL-1β triggered reactivation is via increasing neuronal activity.
source: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels by TTX resulted in a significant decrease in the ability of IL-1β to induce reactivation (Figure 7E), therefore indicating that IL-1β triggered reactivation is via increasing neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that TTX blocks IL-1β-mediated reactivation.

claim: The addition of the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511 blocked reactivation in response to IL-1β.
source: Importantly, the addition of the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511 blocked reactivation in response to IL-1β (Figure 7C) and the role for DLK was confirmed by shRNA mediated depletion (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The role for DLK in IL-1β-mediated reactivation was confirmed by shRNA mediated depletion.
source: Importantly, the addition of the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511 blocked reactivation in response to IL-1β (Figure 7C) and the role for DLK was confirmed by shRNA mediated depletion (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: IL-1β can induce sympathetic neurons to become hyperexcitable and trigger HSV-1 reactivation via activation of DLK.
source: Therefore, IL-1β can induce sympathetic neurons to become hyperexcitable and trigger HSV-1 reactivation via activation of DLK.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that IL-1β induces hyperexcitability and reactivation that is blocked by DLK inhibition.

claim: Hyperexcitability induces HSV to undergo reactivation in a DLK/JNK-dependent manner.
source: Here we show that this state of hyperexcitability induces HSV to undergo reactivation in a DLK/JNK-dependent manner, indicating that the virus responds to both activation of cell stress signaling and prolonged hyperexcitability via a common pathway to result in reactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The virus responds to both activation of cell stress signaling and prolonged hyperexcitability via a common pathway to result in reactivation.
source: Here we show that this state of hyperexcitability induces HSV to undergo reactivation in a DLK/JNK-dependent manner, indicating that the virus responds to both activation of cell stress signaling and prolonged hyperexcitability via a common pathway to result in reactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The common pathway of DLK/JNK activation permits viral lytic gene expression from silenced promoters without the requirement of histone demethylase activity via a histone methyl/phospho switch.
source: This common pathway also permits viral lytic gene expression from silenced promoters without the requirement of histone demethylase activity via a histone methyl/phospho switch.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that Phase I gene expression is independent of histone demethylase activity.

claim: IL-1β induces DNA damage and histone H3 phosphorylation in sympathetic neurons, which are both markers of neuronal excitability.
source: Consistent with this, here we show that IL-1β induces DNA damage and histone H3 phosphorylation in sympathetic neurons, which are both markers of neuronal excitability, and causes increased responses to neurotransmitter stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p following IL-1β treatment.

claim: IL-1β causes increased responses to neurotransmitter stimulation in sympathetic neurons.
source: Consistent with this, here we show that IL-1β induces DNA damage and histone H3 phosphorylation in sympathetic neurons, which are both markers of neuronal excitability, and causes increased responses to neurotransmitter stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased cytosolic Ca2+ in response to acetylcholine following IL-1β treatment.

claim: This study identifies a physiological stimulus that induces HSV reactivation via increasing neuronal excitability.
source: Therefore, this study identifies a physiological stimulus that induces HSV reactivation via increasing neuronal excitability and places DLK/JNK signaling and a histone phospho/methyl switch as central to HSV reactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: DLK/JNK signaling and a histone phospho/methyl switch are central to HSV reactivation.
source: Therefore, this study identifies a physiological stimulus that induces HSV reactivation via increasing neuronal excitability and places DLK/JNK signaling and a histone phospho/methyl switch as central to HSV reactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
